title: Houses at Murnau

image.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Bequest of Katharine Kuh
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Art Institute of Chicago's Open Access program

altText: A small painting of houses in the village of Murnau, Germany, in bold, bright color with simplified shapes. The colors are strong and not meant to match what a camera would see.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist (Vasily Kandinsky, born Moscow, died Neuilly-sur-Seine 1944), date, medium, place of origin, credit line, image id and public-domain flag (true) read from the record. The record has no description or subject terms.

context: Painted in 1909 by Vasily Kandinsky, who was born in Moscow and worked in Germany. Murnau is a town in Bavaria, southern Germany, where Kandinsky painted in these years. The museum record lists oil on cardboard and gives no description.

descriptions.k: These are houses in a village. The colors are bold and bright, not like a photograph. The painter used simple shapes. Which house would you like to visit? What color would you paint your door?
descriptions.g12: Vasily Kandinsky painted houses in a village called Murnau, in Germany. He used bold colors and simple shapes, not tiny details. The painting is small and made on cardboard. Which colors look the happiest? Which house stands out?
descriptions.g35: Vasily Kandinsky, born in Moscow, painted Houses at Murnau in 1909. Murnau is a town in Germany where he painted. He used strong colors and simple shapes instead of copying what he saw exactly, and he worked on cardboard. How do the colors make the houses feel alive? What do you think he wanted to show?
descriptions.g68: Kandinsky painted Houses at Murnau in 1909 on oil and cardboard, using bold color and simplified shapes to show a Bavarian village. The museum gives no description, so look at the evidence: how color, not detail, builds the scene. How do the strong colors express mood, and why might an artist who later painted abstractly begin by simplifying a real place?
descriptions.g910: Houses at Murnau (1909) belongs to the years when Kandinsky, working in Germany, used saturated color and simplified forms to move away from naturalistic description. The museum offers no commentary, so interpretation rests on what is visible. Consider how color acts as feeling rather than record, and how a village scene may mark a step toward the abstraction for which Kandinsky is known.
descriptions.g1112: Houses at Murnau (1909) captures Kandinsky at a turning point, using heightened color and simplified form on a small cardboard support to treat a German village as a field of chromatic relationships. The museum record gives only date, medium and title. How does the painting hold representation and abstraction in tension, and what should we claim about its role in his path to abstraction without overreading?

safety.method: Title, artist and medium checked against the Art Institute of Chicago record; a village scene by title with no concerning terms. The record has no description, so student text relies on the title and well-established facts about Kandinsky and Murnau; a person must confirm the image before release. The image itself was not visually inspected.

teacherNote.context: A 1909 oil painting on cardboard by Vasily Kandinsky in the Art Institute of Chicago, titled for the town of Murnau in Germany. The museum record gives no description, so a person must review the image.
directions: Have students paint their street in unrealistic but expressive colors.
Compare a photograph of a village with this painting and list what Kandinsky changed.
Discuss how an artist can show feeling through color rather than detail.
